advisory.title: Missing dot-stuffing after a bare LF or CR allows SMTP command injection
advisory.description:
Someone who controls the content of a message with bare LF or CR line endings
can end it early with `\n.\n` on a server that takes a bare LF for a line
ending. What follows is read by the server as SMTP commands, which can be used
to send other messages over the same authenticated connection.

This affects messages passed to `send_raw`, and message bodies that are sent
without being encoded. The LF line endings of a `String` body are converted to
CRLF before it is sent.

advisory.title: Unbounded buffering of an SMTP reply allows a malicious server to exhaust memory
advisory.description:
A malicious or compromised server can send a reply line that never ends, which
the client buffers until memory runs out. A reply made of many short lines also
keeps a CPU core busy: for a few seconds per reply since 0.11.22, for as long
as the server wants before it.

Applications that connect only to a trusted server over implicit TLS are not
exposed; the risk applies to clients that may connect to untrusted servers, or
that use `STARTTLS` or no TLS, where a man-in-the-middle can forge the reply.

advisory.title: Panic on a mailbox display name containing CR or LF allows denial of service
advisory.description:
A `Mailbox` whose display name contains a CR or LF panics when it is formatted
or put in a header such as `From` or `To`. Someone who can choose a display
name, for example the name of a user a message is sent to, can crash the
thread or task building the message.

Applications that take display names only from trusted input are not exposed.

advisory.title: Panic on an `EHLO` reply line of only white space allows denial of service
advisory.description:
A malicious or compromised server can reply to `EHLO` with a line holding
nothing but white space, causing the client to panic.

Applications that connect only to a trusted server over implicit TLS are not
exposed; the risk applies to clients that may connect to untrusted servers, or
that use `STARTTLS` or no TLS, where a man-in-the-middle can forge the reply.

advisory.title: Messages for an address with a quoted local part are sent to a different address
advisory.description:
A message whose sender or recipient has a quoted local part is sent with a
different address in its envelope than the one the application was given:
`"d "@example.com` becomes `d@example.com`. Someone who can choose such an
address can have a message delivered to another mailbox than the one the
application validated.

Addresses without a quoted local part are not affected.

advisory.title: STARTTLS response injection allows a man-in-the-middle to forge SMTP replies
advisory.description:
A man-in-the-middle can append replies of their own to the cleartext reply to
`STARTTLS`. The client takes them for the server's replies to the commands it
then sends over TLS, so the attacker can, for example, make a message that the
server rejected look accepted.

Only connections upgraded with `STARTTLS` are affected (`Tls::Required` and
`Tls::Opportunistic`, as set up by `starttls_relay`). Implicit TLS
(`Tls::Wrapper`, as set up by `relay`) is not.

advisory.title: TLS hostname verification disabled when using Boring TLS backend
advisory.description:
An inverted-boolean bug in lettre's `boring-tls` integration silently
disables TLS hostname verification for callers using the default (strict)
configuration. An on-path attacker presenting any chain-valid certificate
for any domain can intercept SMTP submission, including PLAIN/LOGIN
credentials and message contents, against any lettre user built with the
`boring-tls` feature. Other TLS backends (`native-tls`, `rustls`) are
unaffected.

The bug was introduced in v0.10.1 and persists through v0.11.21 (latest).

advisory.title: SMTP command injection in body
advisory.description:
Affected versions of lettre allowed SMTP command injection through an attacker's controlled message body. The module for escaping lines starting with a period wouldn't catch a period that was placed after a double CRLF sequence, allowing the attacker to end the current message and write arbitrary SMTP commands after it.

The flaw is fixed by correctly handling consecutive CRLF sequences.

advisory.title: Argument injection in sendmail transport
advisory.description:
Affected versions of lettre allowed argument injection
to the sendmail command. It was possible, using forged `to` addresses,
to pass arbitrary arguments to the sendmail executable.

Depending on the implementation (original sendmail, postfix, exim, etc.)
it could be possible in some cases to write email data into arbitrary files (using sendmail's
logging features).
 
The flaw is corrected by modifying the executed command to stop parsing arguments
before passing the destination addresses.

NOTE: This vulnerability only affects the `sendmail` transport. Others, including `smtp`, are not
affected.

This vulnerability was reported by vin01.
